# Poincaré–Lefschetz Duality for $(M,\partial M)$

## 1. The three duality maps

Let $M$ be a compact oriented $n$-manifold with $\partial M\neq\varnothing$, and let $i:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$, $j:(M,\varnothing)\hookrightarrow (M,\partial M)$ be the inclusions. The orientation of $M$ gives the relative fundamental class
$$[M,\partial M]\in H_n(M,\partial M;\mathbf Z),\qquad \partial[M,\partial M]=[\partial M]\in H_{n-1}(\partial M;\mathbf Z),$$
where $[\partial M]$ is the induced fundamental class of the closed oriented $(n-1)$-manifold $\partial M$.

Cap product with $[M,\partial M]$ defines two homomorphisms (the **Poincaré–Lefschetz duality maps**):
$$D_0:H^k(M,\partial M;\mathbf Z)\longrightarrow H_{n-k}(M;\mathbf Z),\qquad \alpha\mapsto \alpha\frown [M,\partial M],$$
$$D_1:H^k(M;\mathbf Z)\longrightarrow H_{n-k}(M,\partial M;\mathbf Z),\qquad \beta\mapsto \beta\frown [M,\partial M],$$
using the two cap-product pairings
$$H^k(M,\partial M)\times H_n(M,\partial M)\to H_{n-k}(M),\qquad H^k(M)\times H_n(M,\partial M)\to H_{n-k}(M,\partial M).$$
On the boundary, ordinary Poincaré duality for the **closed** oriented $(n-1)$-manifold $\partial M$ gives
$$D_\partial:H^k(\partial M;\mathbf Z)\longrightarrow H_{n-1-k}(\partial M;\mathbf Z),\qquad \gamma\mapsto \gamma\frown[\partial M].$$

## 2. The duality diagram

Write the long exact sequences of the pair $(M,\partial M)$ in cohomology (top, degree $k$) and in homology (bottom, degree $n-k$), connected by the vertical duality maps:

$$\require{AMScd}
\begin{CD}
\cdots @>>> H^k(M,\partial M) @>>> H^k(M) @>>> H^k(\partial M) @>{\delta}>> H^{k+1}(M,\partial M) @>>> \cdots\\
@. @V{D_0}VV @V{D_1}VV @V{D_\partial}VV @V{D_0}VV @. \\
\cdots @>>> H_{n-k}(M) @>>> H_{n-k}(M,\partial M) @>{\partial}>> H_{n-1-k}(\partial M) @>{i_*}>> H_{n-1-k}(M) @>>> \cdots
\end{CD}$$

(With the conventional sign $(−1)^k$ absorbed into $D_\partial$, the diagram commutes *strictly*; without that convention it commutes up to the standard sign $(−1)^k$.)

## 3. Commutativity

### Square (A): the inclusion square
$$\begin{CD} H^k(M,\partial M) @>{j^*}>> H^k(M) \\ @V{D_0}VV @V{D_1}VV \\ H_{n-k}(M) @>{j_*}>> H_{n-k}(M,\partial M) \end{CD}$$

For $\alpha\in H^k(M,\partial M)$ and $z=[M,\partial M]\in H_n(M,\partial M)$, **naturality of the cap product** with respect to the map of pairs $j:(M,\varnothing)\to(M,\partial M)$ reads
$$j_*\bigl((j^*\alpha)\frown z\bigr)=\alpha\frown j_*z.$$
Since $j_*z=[M,\partial M]=z$, the right side is $\alpha\frown z=j_*(\alpha\frown z)=j_*(D_0\alpha)$. Hence $j_*D_0\alpha=D_1(j^*\alpha)$, i.e. $D_1\circ j^*=j_*\circ D_0$. ∎

### Square (B): the boundary square
$$\begin{CD} H^k(M) @>{i^*}>> H^k(\partial M) \\ @V{D_1}VV @V{D_\partial}VV \\ H_{n-k}(M,\partial M) @>{\partial}>> H_{n-1-k}(\partial M) \end{CD}$$

The fundamental **cap–boundary identity** (see Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, §3.3, or Dold, *Lectures on Algebraic Topology*, VII.12) states that for $c\in H^k(M)$ and $z\in H_n(M,\partial M)$,
$$\partial(c\frown z)=(-1)^k\,(i^*c)\frown \partial z.$$
Taking $z=[M,\partial M]$ and using $\partial[M,\partial M]=[\partial M]$:
$$\partial(D_1 c)=(-1)^k\,(i^*c)\frown[\partial M]=(-1)^k\,D_\partial(i^*c).$$
After redefining $D_\partial$ by the harmless factor $(−1)^k$ (which is the standard convention), this is exactly $\partial\circ D_1=D_\partial\circ i^*$. ∎

### Square (C): the connecting-homomorphism square
$$\begin{CD} H^k(\partial M) @>{\delta}>> H^{k+1}(M,\partial M) \\ @V{D_\partial}VV @V{D_0}VV \\ H_{n-1-k}(\partial M) @>{i_*}>> H_{n-1-k}(M) \end{CD}$$

The companion identity to (B), obtained by applying the cap–boundary relation to a relative cocycle representing $\delta\gamma$ (or equivalently by chasing the cochain-level formula $(\delta\gamma)\frown z=i_*(\gamma\frown\partial z)$, see Hatcher Prop. 3.10 / Dold VII.12.17), gives for $\gamma\in H^k(\partial M)$ and $z\in H_n(M,\partial M)$:
$$(\delta\gamma)\frown z=i_*(\gamma\frown\partial z)$$
(up to the same sign $(−1)^k$, absorbed into $D_\partial$). With $z=[M,\partial M]$ and $\partial z=[\partial M]$:
$$D_0(\delta\gamma)=(\delta\gamma)\frown[M,\partial M]=i_*(\gamma\frown[\partial M])=i_*(D_\partial\gamma),$$
i.e. $D_0\circ\delta=i_*\circ D_\partial$. ∎

Thus the entire diagram commutes: the cohomology LES of $(M,\partial M)$ and the homology LES of $(M,\partial M)$ (with degrees reversed by $k\leftrightarrow n-k$) are identified degree-by-degree through the duality maps.

## 4. Why the vertical maps are isomorphisms

### $D_\partial$ — Poincaré duality on $\partial M$
The boundary $\partial M$ is a **closed** (compact, $\partial(\partial M)=\varnothing$) oriented $(n-1)$-manifold, oriented so that $[\partial M]=\partial[M,\partial M]$. The map $D_\partial:\gamma\mapsto\gamma\frown[\partial M]$ is the classical **Poincaré duality isomorphism**
$$H^k(\partial M;\mathbf Z)\xrightarrow{\;\cong\;}H_{n-1-k}(\partial M;\mathbf Z).$$

### $D_0$ and $D_1$ — Poincaré–Lefschetz duality
These are isomorphisms by the **Poincaré–Lefschetz duality theorem**. The proof reduces to the closed case and proceeds by induction on the complexity of $M$:

**Base case — the $n$-ball.** Let $M=D^n$ with $\partial M=S^{n-1}$. Then $H_n(D^n,S^{n-1})\cong\mathbf Z$ generated by $[D^n,S^{n-1}]$, $H_0(D^n)\cong\mathbf Z$, and all other (co)homology groups vanish. Concretely:
- $D_0:H^n(D^n,S^{n-1})\to H_0(D^n)$ sends the orientation class $\mu\in H^n(D^n,S^{n-1})$ to $\mu\frown[D^n,S^{n-1}]$, a generator of $H_0(D^n)\cong\mathbf Z$. ✓
- $D_1:H^0(D^n)\to H_n(D^n,S^{n-1})$ sends $1$ to $1\frown[D^n,S^{n-1}]=[D^n,S^{n-1}]$, a generator. ✓

Both are isomorphisms (the only nontrivial ones, in degrees $0\leftrightarrow n$); in all other degrees both sides are $0$.

**Inductive step — Mayer–Vietoris and the five-lemma.** Every compact $n$-manifold with boundary admits a finite handle decomposition (equivalently, a finite cover by coordinate balls/half-balls together with a collaring of $\partial M$). Write $M=M_1\cup M_2$ where $M_1,M_2,M_1\cap M_2$ are "simpler" compact manifolds with boundary (e.g. fewer handles). The Mayer–Vietoris sequences for cohomology and for homology, together with the naturality squares (A)–(C) above, produce a morphism of long exact sequences
$$\begin{CD} \cdots @>>> H^k(M_1\cap M_2,\partial) @>>> H^k(M_1,\partial)\oplus H^k(M_2,\partial) @>>> H^k(M,\partial) @>>> \cdots \\ @V{\cong}VV @V{\cong}VV @V{D_0}VV \\ \cdots @>>> H_{n-k}(M_1\cap M_2) @>>> H_{n-k}(M_1)\oplus H_{n-k}(M_2) @>>> H_{n-k}(M) @>>> \cdots \end{CD}$$
The outer vertical maps are isomorphisms by the inductive hypothesis; the **five-lemma** forces the middle map $D_0$ to be an isomorphism. The identical argument with $D_1$ (using the absolute-cohomology/relative-homology Mayer–Vietoris sequence) shows $D_1$ is an isomorphism.

**Equivalent reduction via the double.** Alternatively, form the **double** $DM=M\cup_{\partial M}\overline{M}$ (two copies glued along $\partial M$, the second with reversed orientation); $DM$ is a *closed* oriented $n$-manifold. By excision,
$$H^k(M,\partial M)\cong H^k(DM,\overline{M}),\qquad H_k(M,\partial M)\cong H_k(DM,\overline{M}),$$
and the Poincaré duality isomorphism $H^k(DM,\overline{M})\xrightarrow{\cong}H_{n-k}(M)$ for the closed manifold $DM$ (cap with $[DM]$, restricted via excision) is exactly $D_0$; similarly $D_1$ is obtained from $H^k(M)\cong H^k(DM,\overline{M})\xrightarrow{\cong}H_{n-k}(M,\partial M)$. Thus PL duality for $M$ is literally Poincaré duality for the closed double, transported through excision.

## 5. Conclusion

The Poincaré–Lefschetz duality manifests as a **degree-reversing isomorphism of long exact sequences**: the cohomology LES of the pair $(M,\partial M)$ and the homology LES of $(M,\partial M)$ are identified, degree by degree, by the three vertical cap-product maps
$$D_0:H^k(M,\partial M)\cong H_{n-k}(M),\quad D_1:H^k(M)\cong H_{n-k}(M,\partial M),\quad D_\partial:H^k(\partial M)\cong H_{n-1-k}(\partial M).$$

- **Commutativity** follows from naturality of the cap product (square A) and the cap–boundary identities $\partial(c\frown z)=(-1)^k(i^*c)\frown\partial z$ and $(\delta\gamma)\freen z=i_*(\gamma\frown\partial z)$ (squares B, C), using $\partial[M,\partial M]=[\partial M]$.
- **The vertical maps are isomorphisms** because $D_\partial$ is Poincaré duality for the closed oriented manifold $\partial M$, and $D_0,D_1$ are the Poincaré–Lefschetz duality isomorphisms, proved by verifying the ball as base case and propagating via Mayer–Vietoris and the five-lemma (or, equivalently, by reducing to Poincaré duality on the closed double $DM$ through excision).

In particular, the boundary map $\delta$ in cohomology is identified (up to the conventional sign) with the inclusion $i_*$ in homology, and the restriction $i^*$ in cohomology is identified with the boundary map $\partial$ in homology — exactly the content of the commutative diagram.

# Poincaré–Lefschetz Duality for $(M,\partial M)$

## 1. The three duality maps

Let $M$ be a compact oriented $n$-manifold with $\partial M\neq\varnothing$, and let $i:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$, $j:(M,\varnothing)\hookrightarrow (M,\partial M)$ be the inclusions. The orientation of $M$ gives the relative fundamental class
$$[M,\partial M]\in H_n(M,\partial M;\mathbf Z),\qquad \partial[M,\partial M]=[\partial M]\in H_{n-1}(\partial M;\mathbf Z),$$
where $[\partial M]$ is the induced fundamental class of the closed oriented $(n-1)$-manifold $\partial M$.

Cap product with $[M,\partial M]$ defines two homomorphisms (the **Poincaré–Lefschetz duality maps**):
$$D_0:H^k(M,\partial M;\mathbf Z)\longrightarrow H_{n-k}(M;\mathbf Z),\qquad \alpha\mapsto \alpha\frown [M,\partial M],$$
$$D_1:H^k(M;\mathbf Z)\longrightarrow H_{n-k}(M,\partial M;\mathbf Z),\qquad \beta\mapsto \beta\frown [M,\partial M],$$
using the two cap-product pairings
$$H^k(M,\partial M)\times H_n(M,\partial M)\to H_{n-k}(M),\qquad H^k(M)\times H_n(M,\partial M)\to H_{n-k}(M,\partial M).$$
On the boundary, ordinary Poincaré duality for the **closed** oriented $(n-1)$-manifold $\partial M$ gives
$$D_\partial:H^k(\partial M;\mathbf Z)\longrightarrow H_{n-1-k}(\partial M;\mathbf Z),\qquad \gamma\mapsto \gamma\frown[\partial M].$$

## 2. The duality diagram

Write the long exact sequences of the pair $(M,\partial M)$ in cohomology (top, degree $k$) and in homology (bottom, degree $n-k$), connected by the vertical duality maps:

$$\require{AMScd}
\begin{CD}
\cdots @>>> H^k(M,\partial M) @>>> H^k(M) @>>> H^k(\partial M) @>{\delta}>> H^{k+1}(M,\partial M) @>>> \cdots\\
@. @V{D_0}VV @V{D_1}VV @V{D_\partial}VV @V{D_0}VV @. \\
\cdots @>>> H_{n-k}(M) @>>> H_{n-k}(M,\partial M) @>{\partial}>> H_{n-1-k}(\partial M) @>{i_*}>> H_{n-1-k}(M) @>>> \cdots
\end{CD}$$

(With the conventional sign $(−1)^k$ absorbed into $D_\partial$, the diagram commutes *strictly*; without that convention it commutes up to the standard sign $(−1)^k$.)

## 3. Commutativity

### Square (A): the inclusion square
$$\begin{CD} H^k(M,\partial M) @>{j^*}>> H^k(M) \\ @V{D_0}VV @V{D_1}VV \\ H_{n-k}(M) @>{j_*}>> H_{n-k}(M,\partial M) \end{CD}$$

For $\alpha\in H^k(M,\partial M)$ and $z=[M,\partial M]\in H_n(M,\partial M)$, **naturality of the cap product** with respect to the map of pairs $j:(M,\varnothing)\to(M,\partial M)$ reads
$$j_*\bigl((j^*\alpha)\frown z\bigr)=\alpha\frown j_*z.$$
Since $j_*z=[M,\partial M]=z$, the right side is $\alpha\frown z=j_*(\alpha\frown z)=j_*(D_0\alpha)$. Hence $j_*D_0\alpha=D_1(j^*\alpha)$, i.e. $D_1\circ j^*=j_*\circ D_0$. ∎

### Square (B): the boundary square
$$\begin{CD} H^k(M) @>{i^*}>> H^k(\partial M) \\ @V{D_1}VV @V{D_\partial}VV \\ H_{n-k}(M,\partial M) @>{\partial}>> H_{n-1-k}(\partial M) \end{CD}$$

The fundamental **cap–boundary identity** (see Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, §3.3, or Dold, *Lectures on Algebraic Topology*, VII.12) states that for $c\in H^k(M)$ and $z\in H_n(M,\partial M)$,
$$\partial(c\frown z)=(-1)^k\,(i^*c)\frown \partial z.$$
Taking $z=[M,\partial M]$ and using $\partial[M,\partial M]=[\partial M]$:
$$\partial(D_1 c)=(-1)^k\,(i^*c)\frown[\partial M]=(-1)^k\,D_\partial(i^*c).$$
After redefining $D_\partial$ by the harmless factor $(−1)^k$ (which is the standard convention), this is exactly $\partial\circ D_1=D_\partial\circ i^*$. ∎

### Square (C): the connecting-homomorphism square
$$\begin{CD} H^k(\partial M) @>{\delta}>> H^{k+1}(M,\partial M) \\ @V{D_\partial}VV @V{D_0}VV \\ H_{n-1-k}(\partial M) @>{i_*}>> H_{n-1-k}(M) \end{CD}$$

The companion identity to (B), obtained by applying the cap–boundary relation to a relative cocycle representing $\delta\gamma$ (or equivalently by chasing the cochain-level formula $(\delta\gamma)\frown z=i_*(\gamma\frown\partial z)$, see Hatcher Prop. 3.10 / Dold VII.12.17), gives for $\gamma\in H^k(\partial M)$ and $z\in H_n(M,\partial M)$:
$$(\delta\gamma)\frown z=i_*(\gamma\frown\partial z)$$
(up to the same sign $(−1)^k$, absorbed into $D_\partial$). With $z=[M,\partial M]$ and $\partial z=[\partial M]$:
$$D_0(\delta\gamma)=(\delta\gamma)\frown[M,\partial M]=i_*(\gamma\frown[\partial M])=i_*(D_\partial\gamma),$$
i.e. $D_0\circ\delta=i_*\circ D_\partial$. ∎

Thus the entire diagram commutes: the cohomology LES of $(M,\partial M)$ and the homology LES of $(M,\partial M)$ (with degrees reversed by $k\leftrightarrow n-k$) are identified degree-by-degree through the duality maps.

## 4. Why the vertical maps are isomorphisms

### $D_\partial$ — Poincaré duality on $\partial M$
The boundary $\partial M$ is a **closed** (compact, $\partial(\partial M)=\varnothing$) oriented $(n-1)$-manifold, oriented so that $[\partial M]=\partial[M,\partial M]$. The map $D_\partial:\gamma\mapsto\gamma\frown[\partial M]$ is the classical **Poincaré duality isomorphism**
$$H^k(\partial M;\mathbf Z)\xrightarrow{\;\cong\;}H_{n-1-k}(\partial M;\mathbf Z).$$

### $D_0$ and $D_1$ — Poincaré–Lefschetz duality
These are isomorphisms by the **Poincaré–Lefschetz duality theorem**. The proof reduces to the closed case and proceeds by induction on the complexity of $M$:

**Base case — the $n$-ball.** Let $M=D^n$ with $\partial M=S^{n-1}$. Then $H_n(D^n,S^{n-1})\cong\mathbf Z$ generated by $[D^n,S^{n-1}]$, $H_0(D^n)\cong\mathbf Z$, and all other (co)homology groups vanish. Concretely:
- $D_0:H^n(D^n,S^{n-1})\to H_0(D^n)$ sends the orientation class $\mu\in H^n(D^n,S^{n-1})$ to $\mu\frown[D^n,S^{n-1}]$, a generator of $H_0(D^n)\cong\mathbf Z$. ✓
- $D_1:H^0(D^n)\to H_n(D^n,S^{n-1})$ sends $1$ to $1\frown[D^n,S^{n-1}]=[D^n,S^{n-1}]$, a generator. ✓

Both are isomorphisms (the only nontrivial ones, in degrees $0\leftrightarrow n$); in all other degrees both sides are $0$.

**Inductive step — Mayer–Vietoris and the five-lemma.** Every compact $n$-manifold with boundary admits a finite handle decomposition (equivalently, a finite cover by coordinate balls/half-balls together with a collaring of $\partial M$). Write $M=M_1\cup M_2$ where $M_1,M_2,M_1\cap M_2$ are "simpler" compact manifolds with boundary (e.g. fewer handles). The Mayer–Vietoris sequences for cohomology and for homology, together with the naturality squares (A)–(C) above, produce a morphism of long exact sequences
$$\begin{CD} \cdots @>>> H^k(M_1\cap M_2,\partial) @>>> H^k(M_1,\partial)\oplus H^k(M_2,\partial) @>>> H^k(M,\partial) @>>> \cdots \\ @V{\cong}VV @V{\cong}VV @V{D_0}VV \\ \cdots @>>> H_{n-k}(M_1\cap M_2) @>>> H_{n-k}(M_1)\oplus H_{n-k}(M_2) @>>> H_{n-k}(M) @>>> \cdots \end{CD}$$
The outer vertical maps are isomorphisms by the inductive hypothesis; the **five-lemma** forces the middle map $D_0$ to be an isomorphism. The identical argument with $D_1$ (using the absolute-cohomology/relative-homology Mayer–Vietoris sequence) shows $D_1$ is an isomorphism.

**Equivalent reduction via the double.** Alternatively, form the **double** $DM=M\cup_{\partial M}\overline{M}$ (two copies glued along $\partial M$, the second with reversed orientation); $DM$ is a *closed* oriented $n$-manifold. By excision,
$$H^k(M,\partial M)\cong H^k(DM,\overline{M}),\qquad H_k(M,\partial M)\cong H_k(DM,\overline{M}),$$
and the Poincaré duality isomorphism $H^k(DM,\overline{M})\xrightarrow{\cong}H_{n-k}(M)$ for the closed manifold $DM$ (cap with $[DM]$, restricted via excision) is exactly $D_0$; similarly $D_1$ is obtained from $H^k(M)\cong H^k(DM,\overline{M})\xrightarrow{\cong}H_{n-k}(M,\partial M)$. Thus PL duality for $M$ is literally Poincaré duality for the closed double, transported through excision.

## 5. Conclusion

The Poincaré–Lefschetz duality manifests as a **degree-reversing isomorphism of long exact sequences**: the cohomology LES of the pair $(M,\partial M)$ and the homology LES of $(M,\partial M)$ are identified, degree by degree, by the three vertical cap-product maps
$$D_0:H^k(M,\partial M)\cong H_{n-k}(M),\quad D_1:H^k(M)\cong H_{n-k}(M,\partial M),\quad D_\partial:H^k(\partial M)\cong H_{n-1-k}(\partial M).$$
